newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Celltech to drive pipeline hard.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Celltech to drive pipeline hard.

text.p: British drug discovery company Celltech Group Plc said on Wednesday that it was "driving the pipeline hard" to fill the gap left by the failure of septic shock treatment BAYX-1351.
Last week the company saw its value halve after partner Bayer AG said late-stage trials of the drug showed no impact on the often fatal blood poisoning which can set in after surgery and accidents.

"It was a setback for Celltech and Bayer. It was something that was completely unexpected," finance director Peter Allen told Reuters in a telephone interview after interim results. "There was a sense of disappointment and shock but we have got that behind us and we are getting on with it."
Allen said Celltech had "got caught in the glare of the septic shock headlights," but was now keen to ensure "that everything runs as fast as it can."
"We are determined to make sure we are driving the pipeline hard," he said.

The company was already setting up talks with potential partners to pursue BAYX-1351's follow-up drug CDP-571 in Crohn's disease, a chronic condition affecting the small intestine, and rheumatoid arthritis.
Bayer had told Celltech it would definitely return rights to the drug, although formalities had not been completed.

"That will allow us to do a new deal in chronic indications and we should get more out of it. We have got more to offer," Allen said, with safety and efficacy data available on 100 patients from completed Phase II trials in Britain.
He added that encouraging data earlier this month from a rival drug being developed by Centocor Inc for Crohn's provided further support for Celltech's approach.
"Everything else has moved forward pretty much on schedule," Allen said.

The company gave further detail on progress on a drug for acute myeloid leukaemia, CMA676, being developed by American Home Products Corp, which the partners hope could act as a replacement for chemotherapy.

In trials involving 39 patients with the condition, one of the most aggressive forms of bone marrow cancer, Celltech said two had shown a complete response to treatment, while another seven had cleared all leukaemic cells from their blood.
Allen said AHP's Wyeth-Ayerst division was "very excited" about the data and had started Phase II/Phase III trials in 55 patients. Interim results were likely by the end of the year, he said.

Celltech also announced that an asthma and allergy drug being developed with Schering Plough Corp was likely to go into clinical trials in the second half of the year, after considerable delays due to safety concerns.
"It has taken a long time - they have been very cautious," Allen said, adding that this was "a very big market."
Other pipeline highlights include another drug under development with AHP for small-cell lung cancer and ovarian cancer, with trials in both indications now underway.
Allen said details of the failed septic shock drug trial were of "academic interest," but were likely to be made public at the end of the year or early next year.
"We know there was no sign of efficacy - it wasn't even a near miss," he said.

Celltech said the failed drug had cost it between 2 and 2.5 million stg, compared with royalty payments of 15.7 million stg received from Bayer, which is believed to have spent around $150 million on development.
Allen said the failure had vindicated Celltech's decision to seek partners to share development risks and repeated his view that the company would not need to seek further funding from shareholders.
"We go forward with our financial independence well-established and we are confident of the future," he said.
